newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe's soy buyers may take cover ahead of USDA.
newsitem.headline: Europe's soy buyers may take cover ahead of USDA.

text.p: The prospect of key figures from the USDA next Monday is likely to make European meals and feeds buyers cautious this week although there could be a little offtake in nearby soymeal, traders and analysts said on Monday.

The USDA acreage report is due for release on June 30, and is keenly awaited following last week's ending stocks and acreage estimate from Sparks, which fuelled a soybean rally on the Chicago futures market.

"Everyone in Europe is waiting for those figures but just in case they turn out to be bullish, we may see some consumers taking additional soymeal cover for the summer months," Arie van Dijk of statisticians Stigevo said.
Buying would be limited to these months, with consumers not yet willing to take on cover for the winter, he added.
Sparks on Tuesday pegged 1997 U.S. soybean acreage at 67.5 million acres and corn at 81.9 million, compared to the most recent USDA figures of 68.8 million and 81.4 respectively.

It also put the 1996/97 and 1997/98 U.S. soybean ending stocks below USDA's figures. Sparks pegged the 1996/97 ending stocks at 115 milion bushels and 1997/98 stocks at 123 million against USDA's 130 and 240 million bushels.
"We could see a bullish USDA acreage figure," Van Dijk said.
Van Dijk said the coverage needs varied throughout Europe's feed industry -- with larger companies tending to be better covered than the smaller compounders.
In addition, soymeal usage in Europe was at a low ebb, with compounders replacing it in mixes by rapemeal and feed peas.

Old crop European rapemeal prices on the lower Rhine have been also been rising steadily as crushers run down inventories ahead of planned seasonal shutdownds in July, when most carry out annual maintenance.
But traders pointed out that although old crop rapemeal is expensive in the lower Rhine area, material in Salzgitter was ample and trading at a discount of around one mark.
Elsewhere, heavy rainfall throughout Europe was not seen as having any major impact on the continent's grain crops.
Analysts said that if the wet weather continued, there could be delays to the European harvest but they also noted that grain stocks were sufficient to ride out any potential shortage.
